title: Show us the Father (John 14:8–21)
hook: Philip asks, and he says: whoever has seen me has seen the Father

segments.voice: Yesterday, many rooms in the Father's house, and a table where the friends were troubled. Your line was let not your heart be troubled. Did you make room for someone? Day six hundred thirty-two.

Philip is the practical one. Back in chapter six, with a hungry crowd on a hillside, about five thousand men by John's count, Philip was the one who did the math: two hundred pennyworth of bread wouldn't be enough. Now it's the last supper, and Jesus has been talking for a while about going to the Father, about the way, about knowing the Father already. And Philip, still at the table, says the plain thing. Enough talk. Just show us. One look, and we'll be satisfied. It's a very honest request. Today, the answer he gets.

In the King James Bible Philip says: "Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us." It sufficeth us: that would do it. And the reply comes with a little ache in it: "Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father." All those meals and roads and boats, and Philip is still waiting for the real thing to show up. The answer is that it already has. Hold that up against the Hebrew Bible for a moment. Moses once asked to see God's glory, and in Exodus he is told no one can see God's face and live. In its first chapter, John's Gospel struck the same note: no one has seen God at any time, and the Son has made him known. So when Philip asks to see, the Gospel's answer is a person at a table. Watch how he washes feet, who he eats with, how he speaks to a grieving sister: John's claim is that this is what God is like. Christians have built a great deal on this line. Churches that teach the Trinity read it alongside their teaching that the Father and the Son are distinct and yet one God, and theologians have worked long and hard on how to say that well. The turn is there in the scene itself, though. Philip wants a vision in the sky. He's offered a face across the table. Then Jesus promises he won't leave them orphans. The King James says it this way: "I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you." Another helper is coming, he says, who will stay with them. That thread comes back in the days ahead.
screen: `SHOW US THE FATHER, AND IT'S ENOUGH.`
`SO LONG WITH YOU, AND YOU DON'T KNOW ME?`
`NO ONE HAS SEEN GOD; THE SON MAKES HIM KNOWN.`
then, large: `HE THAT HATH SEEN ME HATH SEEN THE FATHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for God's face in kindness. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one scene from the Gospels where Jesus is kind. Washing the disciples' feet. Bending down to write in the dirt. Calling a short man down from a tree. Pick one and let it play slowly. Watch his hands. Watch who he looks at. If you're a Christian, this is what the line says God looks like. If you're learning, simply notice what kind of face the Gospel is describing. If you pray, you can hold that scene before God in silence. The bell holds the time.
Philip. The practical disciple who asked Jesus, show us the Father, and heard that he already had, in Jesus himself.
Your line: seen the father. Today, when someone is kind to you, pause and notice what that kindness shows you about the one who gave it. Day six hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: John 14 is often read at Christian funerals and in the Easter season, and Christians hear in Jesus's reply to Philip a claim at the center of their faith: that in Jesus, God is made known.

fork.setup: you're Philip. Jesus has been talking a long time about the Father. you want something more solid. what do you say?
options: show us the Father, and that'll be enough.
fork.reveal: Philip asks to be shown, and the answer turns him back to the person in front of him: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.

original.note: Greek: show us the Father. deixon is a command: point it out, put it in front of us.

trapdoor: what you thought: Philip asks a question he should have known the answer to.
what it means: Philip wants one clear vision of God, and is pointed to the person he's been eating with all this time.
what a scholar hears: John opened by saying no one has seen God and the Son has made him known (1:18). Philip's request lets that opening come home.
